newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French bond futures failed to match a contract high set on Wednesday and slipped with German bond futures into the close in a move driven largely by technical factors, trader said.

Some traders said the decline in the September bond contract just before the close was the result of fund selling in core European bonds, initially sparked by a U.S. house selling Bund futures, while others said expected demand from local traders melted away, causing stops to be triggered at the day's lows.
Others said they simply used the earlier rally after the closing of a gap on charts to take some profits above 131.

The September contract started the day in cautious mood ahead of a Bundesbank council meeting then a smaller than expected rise in U.S. jobless claims provided the excuse for a dip to close a gap down to 130.84.
A brief rally followed, taking the contract to the day's high of 131.16 and close to yesterday's contract high of 131.24, before it tumbled as low as 130.66 in the last 10 minutes.
Traders said events in Germany were the main focus at the moment with concerns the Bundesbank might eventually try to support the mark with rate rises causing jitters at the short end of the curve.

Analysts said the German central bank would be unlikely to resort to action yet, but concerns about interest rate rises next year left June and September 1998 PIBOR contracts the worst performers for the second day running.

"It looks as though (the Bundesbank) has basically shifted tack. Before there was a green light for rates being on hold, now they're saying there's only an amber light," Sean Shepley, international economist at CS First Bostong said.
"Depending on the extent of further mark weakness they might chose to tighten liquidity in the money market or shift to a variable rate repo," he said.

He said while the declines Euromarks could be partly justified by the Bundesbank statements after its council meeting the economic situation in France argued strongly against any tightening in policy.

"The key question is, is it really credible for European rates to start rising yet. The answer has to be pretty doubtful and the reason has a lot to do with France. It's policy mix is dangerously verging on the deflationary," Shepley said.
Indeed Sonja Gibbs, bond strategist at Nomura International and Stuart Thomson, economist at at Credit Agricole Indosuez, argued that the next move in French rates could be down.

Economist said while there were signs the weak mark may be raising prices in Germany, inflation in France remained subdued, investment sluggish despite an export-led recovery, consumer demand lacklustre and the prospects for job creation limited.
"No, I don't think France is in a position to cope with higher rates at all," Shepley said.
The franc followed the mark to its lowest level for six years against the dollar, touching 6.2000 briefly. It was trading at 6.1675 at 1532 GMT.
The franc was little changed against the mark at 3.3718 compared with 3.3713 late on Wednesday.
